Protein\u2013protein interaction (PPI) p: Protein–protein interaction (PPI) predictors are commonly evaluated with random pair splits, which permit proteins to recur across training and test sets. Constructed negative pairs can introduce a separate bias when their network properties differ systematically from those of positive pairs. We evaluated both mechanisms in the Guo yeast benchmark using protein-novelty-aware splits, MMseqs2 sequence-similarity-controlled variants, handcrafted and frozen protein-language-model representations, topology-only controls, degree-matched putative negatives, multiple architectures, seed analyses, and cluster-aware inference. In the matched protein-novelty curve, AAC+CTD–MLP ROC-AUC declined from 0.697 for seen–seen pairs (R1) to 0.626 for one-unseen pairs (R2) and 0.587 for both-unseen pairs (R3). Additional sequence-identity exclusion from R3-50 to R3-20 produced no consistent monotonic decline. Guo's original negative endpoints had lower positive-network degree than positive endpoints (mean 3.34 versus 6.72). A degree-only logistic model reached ROC-AUC 0.962 on the original negatives and 0.502 on degree-matched negatives. Under consistently trained and evaluated R3 degree-matched data, six sequence-model architectures produced ROC-AUC 0.493–0.547, with no corrected cluster-aware evidence that any exceeded chance. The large N0–N2 point-estimate gap was directionally robust but was not statistically established by the corrected component-aware tests. A separately constructed multi-species benchmark also exhibited degree-associated bias. Its pooled N2 result was additionally confounded by cross-species negative pairing; within-species replication is reported separately. Protein-novelty control and negative-set control therefore address complementary failure modes. The Guo collapse is benchmark-specific and should not be generalized to sequence-based PPI prediction or protein language models overall.
3.7 A second benchmark retains sequence: 3.7 Pooled second-benchmark discrimination after degree control
The independently constructed multi-spec: The independently constructed multi-species benchmark provided a critical specificity test. A degree-only logistic model declined from ROC-AUC 0.849 under N0 to 0.535 under N2, confirming that original negatives also carried degree-associated separability. Sequence models retained pooled N2 discrimination: AAC+CTD–MLP achieved ROC-AUC 0.646, ESM-2 logistic regression 0.682, and ESM-2–MLP 0.698. Exact-degree and nearest-degree matching produced comparable residual sequence discrimination while moving the degree-only model closer to chance.
The multi-species experiment is essentia: The multi-species experiment is essential to the paper's scope. It reproduced degree-associated separability: the degree-only model was strong under N0 and nearly uninformative after matching. At the same time, ESM-2 and AAC+CTD retained meaningful N2 discrimination. However, the taxonomic audit found that 45.1% of pooled N2 negatives joined different species, and a same-species indicator alone achieved ROC-AUC 0.729. The pooled sequence result therefore cannot establish molecular interaction signal independent of taxonomic pairing cues. Section 3.8 reports the within-species controls. The Guo result should not be generalized to all PPI benchmarks, PLMs, or deep learning. Instead, it illustrates why representation claims should be conditional on the negative-set construction and why independent benchmarks should be chosen for methodological diversity rather than treated as interchangeable confirmation sets.
The fifth conclusion concerns generality: The fifth conclusion concerns generality. In the multi-species benchmark, degree-only discrimination again declined strongly after matching, indicating that degree-associated negative-set bias is not unique to Guo. Sequence models retained pooled discrimination under matched negatives, but cross-species negative pairing provided an additional cue. The within-species analyses in Section 3.8 refine this comparison; their single-split estimates do not establish unseen-protein generalization or molecular compatibility. Neither the Guo collapse nor pooled residual discrimination supports a universal claim about protein language models, handcrafted sequence descriptors, or deep architectures. The appropriate lesson is methodological: benchmark controls determine which scientific claims the resulting performance can support.
